30-005.r: Battle of Haldighati (Akbar vs Maharana Pratap) → 1576 A.D.

30-006.r: Commander of Rana Pratap's army at Haldighati → Hakim Khan Sur, a Pathan of the Sur Dynasty, leading about 5,000 Afghans.

30-007.r: Commander-in-chief of the Rajput army besides Maharana Pratap at Haldighati (1576) → Hakim Khan Sur, descendant of Sher Shah Suri, leading Afghans.
30-007.t: Don't pick Man Singh: he led Akbar's side.

30-009.r: Map of Akbar's empire at his death (1605) → 'A' = Gondwana (independent state); 'B' = Lahore (inside the empire).

30-010.r: Akbar's first Rajput marriage alliance → Kachhwahas of Amber: Raja Bihari Mal (Bharmal) submitted at Sanganer (1562), gave daughter Harkhabai.

30-012.r: Akbar often visited → Dargah of Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer and shrine of Shaikh Salim Chishti at Sikri.

30-013.r: Personally killed by Akbar (1562 AD) → Adham Khan, son of Maham Anga, for murdering prime minister Atagh Khan.

30-014.r: Mewar did not accept Akbar's supremacy willingly (Rana Pratap fought on); his son Rana Amar Singh signed a treaty with Jahangir in 1615 A.D.

30-015.r: Rao Chandrasena of Marwar → never surrendered to the Mughals (like Rana Pratap); fought at Bhadrajun 1571, took Sojat 1579, died January 1581.

30-016.r: Rani Durgavati → ruled Gondwana for minor son Vir Narayan; fought Akbar's army, defeated between Garh and Mandla (Mandla district, M.P.).

30-017.r: Abul Fazl killed while returning from Deccan (called back 1602) → by Vir Singh Bundela, in a plot of rebel Prince Salim at Allahabad.

30-018.r: Not a factor making Akbar a nationalist → 'Akbar had forsaken Islam' (untrue); religious tolerance, administrative and legal unity, cultural unity were factors.

30-019.r: Akbar's popularity → Mansabdari system, religious policy, land revenue system and social reforms (all four); he also abolished the pilgrimage tax.

30-021.r: 'Enlightened despot' → Akbar: liberal and tolerant but held complete authority; compared with Queen Elizabeth I and Frederick the Great.

30-022.r: Chronology → Mughal invasion of Malwa (1561) – Akbar marries Amber princess (1562) – Karrani's conquest of Orissa (1568) – Battle of Tukaroi (1575).

30-023.r: Akbar → one wife per man, a second only if the first was barren; also encouraged widow remarriage and discouraged Sati.

30-024.r: Akbar → fixed marriage age (girls 14, boys at least 16) and let girls marry by their own will, not parental pressure; both true.

30-025.r: Akbar's reign → annexations, provincial administration, judicial administration; NOT religious intolerance (he followed 'Sulh-i-Kul').

30-026.r: Head of Akbar's military department → Mir Bakshi (not chief commander); handled recruitment, ranks, pay and inspection of mansabdars.
30-026.t: Don't confuse Mir Bakshi (military) with Diwan (finance) or Mir Saman (household).

30-027.r: Akbar's military system → Mansabdari (1574-75), after reviving Chehra (soldier's descriptive roll) and Dagh (horse branding) in 1573-74.

30-028.r: Mansabdari system introduced, per this question → to ensure clean administration.
30-028.t: BPSC key chose 'clean administration' over 'army recruitment' or 'revenue collection'.

30-029.r: First proper Diwan of Akbar → Muzaffar Khan Turbati (Todar Mal as assistant); the Diwan's department grew from his appointment.

30-030.r: Akbar's Mansabdari system → borrowed from Mongolia, based on the Mongol army division under Genghis Khan.

30-031.r: Akbar's mansabdars kept twenty horses per ten cavalrymen → horses needed rest on march and replacement in war; A and R true, R explains A.

30-032.r: Zabti system → Akbar: measurement-based land revenue; revenue circles (dasturs) with per-bigha cash rates; Ain-i-Dahsala (ten-year average).

30-033.r: Todarmal → famous for land revenue: Dahsala or Zabti system (1580 A.D.), called 'Todarmal settlement', based on ten-year average produce and prices.

30-034.r: Bandobast system → Dahsala, Akbar's land revenue system.

30-035.r: Todarmal → land revenue reforms: one-third of the ten-year average produce (1571-1580 AD) fixed as state revenue = Dahsala ('Todarmal Bandobast').

30-036.r: Only true: Abul Fazl wrote Ain-i-Akbari. Tansen title came from king of Gwalior/Rewa; Jahangir (not Akbar) married Man Singh's sister; Todarmal headed revenue, not army.

30-037.r: Link between Sher Shah and Akbar in land revenue → Raja Todarmal, main propounder of Ain-i-Dahsala ('Todarmal Settlement'), helped by Shah Mansoor, Muzaffar Khan Turbati.

30-039.r: Din-i-Ilahi (Tauhid-i-Ilahi) → launched by Akbar in 1582 AD; prophet Abul Fazl; only Hindu follower Birbal; Bhagawan Das and Man Singh refused.

30-042.r: Din-i-Ilahi → not a religion but an ideology of Sufi pantheism; neither Abul Fazl, Badauni nor Nizamuddin called it one; Mohsin Fani did, in 'Dabistan-i-Mazahib'.

30-043.r: Ibadat Khana, Fatehpur Sikri → built by Akbar in 1575 for religious debates; opened to all religions in 1578; led to Mahzarnama (1579).

30-045.r: Jama Masjid, Fatehpur Sikri → 'Shah-i-Fatehpur' / 'Shan-i-Sikri'; Fatehpur Sikri was the Mughal capital 1571-1585 AD.

30-046.r: Akbari Mahal → in Agra Fort, not Fatehpur Sikri; Fatehpur Sikri has Jodha Bai Mahal, Panch Mahal, Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas, Birbal ki Kothi.

30-047.r: Humayun's Tomb, Delhi → synthesis of Persian and Indian architecture; built under Humayun's wife, designed by Mirak Mirza.

30-048.r: 'Sulh-i-Kul' (universal peace) → Akbar's religious policy of universal harmony; led to his sect Din-i-Ilahi in 1582 A.D.

30-050.r: Fatwa from Jaunpur → against Akbar, issued in 1580 A.D. by Mulla Muhammad Yazdi, asking all Muslims to rebel.

30-051.r: Buland Darwaza, Fatehpur Sikri → Akbar's victory gate for Gujarat (annexed 1572-73), not Jahangir's birth; Percy Brown links it to the South victory (1601).

30-052.r: Buland Darwaja, Fatehpur Sikri → built by Akbar for his victory over Gujarat, not for Jahangir's birth; A true, R false.
30-052.t: Don't link Buland Darwaza with Jahangir's birth; it marks the Gujarat victory.

30-054.r: Built by Akbar → Buland Darwaza and Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri; not Qutb Minar or Taj Mahal.

30-055.r: Educational reforms → Akbar: added arithmetic, logic, geometry, astronomy, accountancy, public administration, agriculture to studies, though he had no formal education.

30-056.r: Akbar's finest monuments → Fatehpur Sikri (Sikri, 37 km from Agra, home of Salim Chishti): Diwan-i-Aam, Diwan-i-Khas, Panch Mahal, Jodha Bai Mahal, Birbal ki Kothi.

30-057.r: Panch Mahal, Fatehpur Sikri → five-storey columnar building like a Buddhist monastery (inspired by Nalanda); plan like a Persian badgir (wind catcher).

30-058.r: Panch Mahal (Akbar, Fatehpur Sikri) → Buddhist-monastery style, five storeys; ground floor has 84 pillars.

30-060.r: Jahangir Mahal → inside Agra Fort (Akbar's fort, chief architect Kasim Khan, red sandstone), built by Akbar for Shahzada Salim.

30-061.r: Akbar's tomb → Sikandara (Bahistabad) near Agra, village founded by Sikandar Lodi; completed by Jahangir in 1613 A.D.; five storeys, domeless top.

30-062.r: Not built under Akbar → Red Fort of Delhi (Shah Jahan, completed 1648 A.D.); Agra, Allahabad and Lahore Forts were Akbar's.

30-063.r: Tombs → Babur: Kabul; Akbar: Sikandara; Jahangir: Lahore; Shah Jahan: Agra.
30-063.t: Akbar's tomb is at Sikandara, not Agra city; Shah Jahan lies in Agra.

30-064.r: Tombs → Babur: Kabul; Humayun: Delhi; Akbar: Sikandara; Jahangir: Lahore.

30-065.r: Persian Mahabharat under Akbar → made under Faizi's direction, with Naqib Khan and Badauni; the Translation Department was under Abul Fazl.

30-066.r: Mahabharata into Persian ('Razmnama', book of Wars) → on Akbar's orders by Faizi, Naqib Khan, Abdul Qadir Badauni and others.

30-067.r: Razmnama → Persian Mahabharata (16th century) by Badauni, Naqib Khan, Faizi; Badauni also translated the Ramayan; Faizi → Leelavati; Abul Fazl → Kaliyadaman.
30-067.h: Razm = war: Razmnama is the war epic, the Mahabharata.

30-072.r: 'Zari Qalam' honour from Akbar → Muhammad Husain of Kashmir, a famous writer of his court.

30-073.r: Jain monk titled 'Jagadguru' by Akbar → Hari Vijay Suri; his non-violence made Akbar turn vegetarian and ban killing of animals and birds.

30-074.r: 'Jagat Guru' title from Akbar → Hir (Hari) Vijay Suri, the Jain scholar Akbar respected.

30-076.r: Akbar's famous painter → Daswant, a potter's son and first artist of his time; Ain-i-Akbari also lists Basawan, Miskin, Mukund, Keshav Lal.

30-077.r: Contemporary of Queen Elizabeth-I (1558-1603) → Akbar (1556-1605); East India Company founded 1600 under Elizabeth.

30-078.r: English East India Company formed (1600 A.D.) → Akbar was emperor of India; Elizabeth was queen of England.

30-079.r: Medieval Indian writer who mentions the discovery of America → Abul Fazl.

30-080.r: First Englishman at Akbar's court → Ralph Fitch (1583-86 A.D.), merchant who visited Agra and Fatehpur Sikri and described 16th-century Indian trade.

30-081.r: Akbar's chronology → Jizya abolished (1564) – Ibadat Khana (1575) – Mahzar (1579, drafted by Shaikh Mubarak) – Din-i-Ilahi (1582).

30-082.r: Goa Church's third mission (1595) → met Akbar at Lahore; led by Jerome Xavier; earlier missions 1580 (Fatehpur Sikri) and 1591 (Lahore).
30-082.c: Book marks all three true, but Antonio Monserrate came with the first mission (1580) and tutored Murad then; the third mission under Jerome Xavier did not include him, so (iii) is false and (b) is right.

30-083.r: Akbar merged Bengal and Bihar → 1576 A.D.: Munim Khan took Bihar (1574) from Daud Khan Karrani; Todarmal defeated Daud on 12 July 1576.

31-001.r: 'Do-aspa Sih-aspa' → Jahangir: mansabdars kept double (do-aspa) or triple (sih-aspa) horses for their sawar rank, without a rise in zat.
31-001.h: Do = two, Sih = three horses per trooper.

31-002.r: Treaty of Chittor (1615 A.D.) → Jahangir's reign: Rana of Mewar accepted Mughal allegiance; Jahangir returned Mewar and Chittorgarh.

31-003.r: First East India Company envoy to Jahangir → William Hawkins (1608-11; mansab of 400); Sir Thomas Roe was the first ambassador of King James-I.

31-005.r: 'English Khan' title from Jahangir → William Hawkins (came 1608), whom Jahangir also pressed to marry an Armenian lady.

31-007.r: Sir Thomas Roe (1615-1619) → ambassador of King James-I in Jahangir's reign, sent to win trade facilities for the British.

31-009.r: Sir Thomas Roe → reached Surat on 18 September 1615 as James-I's ambassador; attended Jahangir's court at Ajmer in 1616.

31-010.r: British ambassador who followed Jahangir from Ajmer to Mandu → Sir Thomas Roe (at court from 1616); also went to Ahmedabad and hunting with him.

31-011.r: Thomas Roe received by Jahangir → at Ajmer, 1616 A.D.; stayed till 1619, then returned with Jahangir's decree welcoming the British.

31-012.r: Arrival order → Ralph Fitch (1583) – William Hawkins (Surat 1608) – Nicholas Dawnton (1614-15) – Sir Thomas Roe (January 1616).

31-013.r: Dutch traveller with a valuable account of Jahangir's reign → Francisco Pelsaert ('Remonstrantie'); Peter Mundy came under Shahjahan; Manucci (Italian) in the succession war.

31-015.r: Mughal emperors with no tomb in India → Babur (Kabul, Afghanistan) and Jahangir (Shahdara, Lahore, Pakistan); both (b) and (d) correct.

31-017.r: Tomb outside India → Jahangir, buried in a tomb garden at Shahdara, Lahore (died 1627 AD).

31-018.r: Mughal painting peaked under Jahangir; titles → Abul Hasan 'Nadir-ul-Zaman' (portraits), Ustad Mansur 'Nadir-ul-Asra' (plants and animals).
31-018.h: Mansur = nature (plants, animals); Hasan = human portraits.

31-023.r: Jahangir's court painters → Manohar, Bishandas, Mansur; Basawan was Akbar's court painter.

31-024.r: Mughal autobiography in Persian → Jahangir's Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri, in three parts; preface written after his death by Muhammad Hadi.

31-025.r: Abul Fazl's killer Raja Vir Singh Bundela → rewarded by Jahangir after his coronation (November 1605; title 'Nuruddin Muhammad Jahangir Badshah Ghazi').

31-026.r: Rebels against Jahangir → Khusrau (1606), Khurram (1622; beaten at Bilochpur 1623), Mahabat Khan (1626); not Asif Khan.

31-027.r: Khusrau → eldest son of Jahangir; mother Man Bai.

31-028.r: Nur Jahan's Junta → Nur Jahan, mother Asmat Begum, father Ghiyas Beg (Itmad-ud-Daula), brother Asaf Khan, Prince Khurram; not Jahangir or Mahabat Khan.

31-030.r: Itmad-ud-Daula's tomb, Agra → built by Nur Jahan (1622-1628 A.D.) for her father, on the Yamuna; first Indian tomb entirely of white marble.

31-031.r: Pietra dura → wall decoration with floral designs of inlaid semi-precious stones; first done in India in Itmad-ud-Daula's tomb (built by Nur Jahan).

31-032.r: Babur → Jama Masjid (Sambhal); Humayun → Din Panah; Akbar → Jahangiri Mahal; Jahangir → completed Akbar's Mausoleum.

31-033.r: Govind Palace (Bir Singh Palace) → Datia (M.P.), seven-storey Bundela building by Raja Bir Singh Deo, 1614 A.D.

31-034.r: Wrong pair → Nizamuddin Auliya's tomb is in Delhi (Ghiyaspur; died 1325), not Ajmer; Akbar → Sikandara; Jahangir → Shahdara; Salim Chishti → Fatehpur Sikri.

32-001.r: Map of an empire without Golconda → Shah Jahan's; Golconda was captured later, by Aurangzeb in 1687.

32-002.r: Root of the Iran–Mughal dispute → Qandahar, for strategic, economic and prestige reasons.

32-003.r: Loss of Qandahar (under Shah Jahan) → blow to a strategic stronghold; it exposed the Mughal empire to outside attacks.

32-004.r: Kavindracharya (Saraswati) → led Banaras pandits to seek abolition of the pilgrim tax on Banaras and Allahabad; poet patronised by Shah Jahan.

32-006.r: Shah Jahan's Balkh campaign → to secure a friendly ruler in Balkh and Badakshan bordering Kabul (a buffer against Persia), not to win Samarqand and Ferghana.

32-007.r: Poet-Laureate of Shah Jahan → Kaleem (Abu Jalih).

32-008.r: Mumtaz Mahal → real name Arjumand Bano Begum, daughter of Asaf Khan, wife of Prince Khurram (Shah Jahan).

32-009.r: Blend of Hindu (Indian) and Iranian architecture → Taj Mahal, built by Shah Jahan with architects from India, Persia and Middle Asia.

32-010.r: Jama Masjid of Delhi → Shah Jahan; his other works: Diwan-e-Aam, Diwan-e-Khas, Sheesh Mahal, Moti Masjid (Agra), Musamman Burj, Nagina Masjid, Taj Mahal, Red Fort.

32-012.r: Capital shifted from Agra to Delhi (Shahjahanabad) → Shah Jahan.

32-013.r: Alai Darwaza, Delhi → Alauddin Khalji; Buland Darwaza → Akbar; Moti Masjid, Agra → Shah Jahan; Moti Masjid, Delhi → Aurangzeb.
32-013.t: Two Moti Masjids: Agra (Shah Jahan) vs Delhi (Aurangzeb).

32-014.r: Red Fort (Lal Qila), Delhi → Shah Jahan, in his new capital Shahjahanabad; irregular octagon with Lahori (west) and Delhi (south) gates.

32-016.r: Upanishads into Persian → Dara Shikoh under Shah Jahan, as 'Sirr-i-Akbar' (about 52 Upanishads); title 'Shah Buland Iqbal'; own work Majma-ul-Bahrain.

32-021.r: Dara Shikoh's original work → Majma-ul-Bahrain (Mazzmaul Bahainna); Sirr-i-Akbar is his Persian translation of the Upanishads.
32-021.c: Option (e) Sirr-i-Akbar is also Dara's (a translation); the book picks his original work (d).

32-022.r: Dara Shikoh (killed 1659 AD) → body buried in Humayun's Tomb complex, Delhi; head said to be buried in the Taj Mahal complex, Agra.

32-023.r: First Muslim (among options) to study Hindu scriptures → Dara Shikoh, Shah Jahan's eldest son; translated Yogvashita and Bhagwad Gita into Persian.

32-024.r: Shah Jahan's reign = 'Golden Era' → A.L. Srivastava ('Mughalkaleen Bharat'), true mainly for art and architecture; J.N. Sarkar and V.A. Smith disagree.

32-025.r: Kohinoor (from Golconda mines) → presented to Shah Jahan by Mir Jumla, Persian noble and diamond dealer, ex-minister of Golconda, titled 'Muazzam Khan'.

32-026.r: Shah Jahan → abolished 'Sijda' (prostration), the Persian court custom begun by Balban.

32-027.r: Governor of Deccan for most of Shah Jahan's reign → Aurangzeb: 1636-44 and 1653-1658 A.D.

33-001.r: Aurangzeb (third son) took Shah Jahan's throne by force; no primogeniture rule (Dara was eldest); A true, R false.

33-002.r: Crowned twice → Aurangzeb: 21 July 1658 (Delhi) and 5 June 1659, after the Khajwa and Deoria victories.

33-003.r: Battle of Dharmat (M.P., 15th April 1658) → Aurangzeb (with Prince Murad) defeated Dara Shikoh's forces under Raja Jaswant Singh.

33-004.r: Chronology → Bilgram (1540, Sher Shah beat Humayun) – Sarnal (1572, Akbar beat Ibrahim Mirza) – Dharmat (1658) – Jajau (1707, Bahadur Shah-I vs Azam Shah).

33-005.r: Dharmat (Aurangzeb beat Jaswant Singh of Jodhpur, 1658) → in Madhya Pradesh.

33-006.r: Succession war order → Shuja defeated near Banaras (February 1658) – Dharmat (15 April 1658) – Samugarh (29 May 1658) – Deorai (1659).

33-007.r: Mughal prince who took refuge in Srinagar (Garhwal) → Sulaiman Shikoh, Dara's son; Medini Shah handed him to Aurangzeb; killed in Gwalior Fort with opium.

33-008.r: Aurangzeb's son who revolted (1681 A.D.), weakening him against the Rajputs → Muhammad Akbar.

33-009.r: Treaty of Purandar (1665 AD) → Shivaji with Raja Jai Singh of Amber, Aurangzeb's general, after the siege of Purandar Fort.
33-009.t: Don't confuse Jai Singh (Purandar) with Jaswant Singh (Dharmat) or Shaista Khan.

33-010.r: 'Zinda Peer' → Aurangzeb, for his high morals and simple life; also called 'Shahi Darvesh'.

33-011.r: 'Zinda Pir' → Aurangzeb, third son of Shah Jahan, emperor 1658-1707 A.D.

33-012.r: None came under Aurangzeb: Peter Mundy → Shah Jahan; William Hawkins, Thomas Roe → Jahangir; Antonio Monserrate → Akbar.
33-012.c: Answer not printed: none of the four options visited in Aurangzeb's reign.

33-013.r: First Mughal to fight the British → Aurangzeb: conflict of 1686 A.D.; governor Shaistha Khan drove the British, including Job Charnock, out of Hooghly.

33-014.r: Aurangzeb's Deccan conquests → Bijapur (1686 A.D.) and Golconda (1687 A.D.).
33-014.h: Alphabetical = chronological: Bijapur first, then Golconda.

33-016.r: Golconda ruler when Aurangzeb took it (1687) → Abul Hasan Qutb Shah; fort opened with 'keys of gold', as Akbar did at Asirgarh.

33-017.r: Map with Bijapur and Golconda inside the empire → Aurangzeb's kingdom at his death, 1707 A.D.

33-018.r: Most Hindu generals/officials → Aurangzeb: 31.6% (mostly Marathas) vs Akbar 22.5% and Shah Jahan 22.4%.

33-020.r: Jizya → abolished by Akbar, re-imposed by Aurangzeb in 1679 A.D. on non-Muslims in three income classes (12, 24, 48 Dirham a year).

33-021.r: Aurangzeb's Jihad → holy war on non-Muslim lands (Dar-ul-Harb) to make them Dar-ul-Islam; key answer: Dar-ul-Islam.
33-021.t: Dar-ul-Harb is the land fought against; Dar-ul-Islam is the goal.

33-022.r: Bibi Ka Maqbara ('Mini Taj', Deccan Taj Mahal) → tomb of Rabia-ud-Daurani, built by her son Azam Shah in Aurangzeb's reign.

33-024.r: Mehrunnisa → daughter of Aurangzeb; Jahan Ara, Roshan Ara and Gauhar Ara were daughters of Shah Jahan.

33-025.r: 'Sahibat-uz-Zamani' → title from Aurangzeb to Jahan Ara, eldest daughter of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal.

33-026.r: Samarth Ramdas (1608-1681 A.D., Maharashtra) → contemporary of Aurangzeb; Guru Ramdas (fourth Sikh guru) was Akbar's contemporary.
33-026.t: Don't confuse Samarth Ramdas (Aurangzeb) with Guru Ramdas (Akbar).

33-027.r: Moti Masjid in the Red Fort, Delhi → Aurangzeb.

34-001.r: Mughal provinces → Subas; districts → Sarkars; sub-districts → Parganas (groups of villages); Sarkar officers: Faujdar, Amalguzar, Qazi, Kotwal.

34-003.r: Head of the military in Mughal period → Mir Bakshi; also handled intelligence and recommended military appointments and promotions.

34-004.r: Mir Bakshi (per this question) → supervised land revenue officials besides military salaries; Jadunath Sarkar called him Pay Master; revenue head was Wazir/Diwan.

34-005.r: Mughal Empire was basically a Military State; the central government's vitality depended on military power; A and R true, R explains A.

34-006.r: Physician in Mughal service → Niccolao Manucci (Italian): first Dara Shikoh's artilleryman, turned doctor after Dara's death in 1659.

34-007.r: Ahadis → Akbar's gentlemen-troopers: served singly, attached to no chief, directly under the emperor; excellent archers with several horses.

34-008.r: Muhtasib → censor of public morals; acted as police-cum-judge for Muslims' observance of canon law.

34-009.r: Mansabdari (Akbar) → introduced mainly for clean and better administration; became the base of Mughal military and civil administration.

34-010.r: Smooth running of Mansabdari → Mir Bakshi; 'Mansab' (Arabic) = rank or position; the system fixed officials' rank, duties and pay.

34-011.r: Mansabdari → 33 classes; all civil and military officers held mansabs; conditional (Mashrut) rank = temporary rise in sawar; key: sawar exceeding zat is 'not true'.

34-012.r: Mansabdari → zat and mansab ranks granted; king appointed mansabdars; not hereditary; 33 categories, from 10 to 10,000 soldiers; key: statements 1 and 3 true.
34-012.c: No conflict: there were 33 grades of mansab, and within each grade mansabdars fell into three classes by sawar rank (equal to zat, at least half of it, or below half).

34-013.r: Both statements wrong: Jagirdars got revenue assignments in lieu of cash salary; police and judicial work was local Zamindars'; jagirs were transferable, Zamindars hereditary.
